                    ### Question
                    A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a dog bite. The patient was intoxicated and pulled the dog’s tail while it was eating. The dog belongs to his friend and is back at his friend’s house currently. Physical exam is notable for a dog bite on the patient’s right arm. The wound is irrigated and explored with no retained bodies found. A tetanus vaccination is administered. Which of the following is appropriate management of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Administer amoxicillin-clavulanic acid
opb. Administer the rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin
opc. Administer trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
opd. Close the wound with sutures and discharge the patient
ope. Discharge the patient with outpatient follow up

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In the case of a dog bite, the management should consider the risk of infection and potential rabies exposure. The patient requires prophylactic antibiotics due to the nature of the bite, and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is the first-line treatment for dog bites to prevent infection. The assessment of rabies exposure is crucial; however, since the dog is known and presumably vaccinated, rabies vaccination and immunoglobulin may not be necessary unless the dog shows signs of rabies or is unvaccinated. Wound closure with sutures is generally not recommended due to the risk of infection, especially in bite wounds. Given that the patient has received a tetanus vaccination, outpatient follow-up is appropriate if no further interventions are needed. Therefore, the most appropriate management option is to administer amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for infection prophylaxis.
